title: RSS and why a studio should keep it
metaTitle: Why a studio should keep an RSS feed
excerpt: A feed lets someone follow the writing without an account. Keep it current when you publish. That is a small promise the work is ongoing.
alt: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony, a long run of volumes a person can follow without asking permission.
caption: Library shelves seen from a balcony, a collection you can keep reading. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is a blog RSS feed for?
faqs.answer: It lets a person follow new writing in a reader they already use, without making an account on your site. Each item should point at a real article, with a title, a date, and a link. It is a subscription that respects the reader more than a popup does.

faqs.question: Should unpublished drafts appear in the feed?
faqs.answer: No. The feed should list only what you have published. A draft, a preview URL, or a portal page does not belong there. If a piece is not ready for a stranger, it is not ready for a subscriber.

faqs.question: How often does the feed need to change?
faqs.answer: Update it when you publish, not on a timer that invents items. A quiet month should look quiet. A feed that repeats old posts to seem active, or that dumps a hundred items in a day, breaks the small promise that the writing is ongoing and cared for.

markdown:
A blog RSS feed is a file that lets a person follow the writing without an account. Keep it current when you publish. That currency is a small promise: the work is ongoing, and the next piece will arrive the same way the last one did.

You do not need a large audience for the promise to be worth keeping. You need a few people who wanted the next essay and should not have to remember to check.

## A follow without an account

Most studio sites ask for attention in a clumsy way. A modal wants an email. A social profile wants a follow on a platform that will bury the post. A feed is quieter. The reader adds the URL to a reader they chose, and new pieces show up beside the other writing they already trust. No password on your site. No "subscribe to our newsletter" that then sends a discount.

That matters for a studio talking to founders. The people you want as clients are already drowning in logins. A feed says you will publish on a page they can open, and you will tell their reader when it exists. It is closer to a shelf in a library than to a campaign. The shelf does not tap them on the shoulder. It is simply there, in order, when they come back.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether you have an audience that would find the content useful if they came to you directly, and whether the site has a primary purpose. A feed is a practical answer to the first question. It is built for people who already decided your writing is worth another visit. It is a bad tool for chasing strangers who have never heard of you, which is a good reason to keep it. The purpose stays narrow: the writing, in order, for people who asked.

The guidance also warns against mass-producing pages, and against adding or removing large amounts of content just to look fresh. A feed makes that temptation visible. Subscribers notice a dump. They notice a week of silence less than you fear, if the previous pieces were finished. They notice a feed that reposts the same URL with a new date and no real change, because their reader flags it as new and the page is not.

## What belongs in an item

Each item needs a title, a link to the official URL, a date, and a short summary that matches the article. The summary can be the excerpt. It should not be a tease, and it should not be the entire essay pasted ten times into a file nobody asked to download in full. A short, true summary respects the reader and the page. The page is where the piece lives. The feed is the notice.

Use the same title the page uses. A feed title that was written for clicks, sitting on an article that was written with care, is two voices. Use the canonical URL, not a preview link, not a tagged campaign link, and not a staging host. If you have just done the work of picking one official address, the feed is the first place that decision should show up. Every subscriber's reader will request that URL. Make it the real one.

Include the author if the author is real. "Admin" in a feed is the same failure as "Admin" on the page. A studio byline is fine when the studio stands behind the piece and the author page explains the practice. A person's name is fine when that person will still be there, and the page about them is true. Do not invent a staff of authors so the feed looks like a magazine.

Dates should be publication dates. If you substantially update a piece, decide whether the item should show the update. A small typo fix does not deserve to jump the queue. A changed recommendation does. Say so in the summary if the reader may have seen the old version. Silent revisions of advice are how a feed loses the trust it was meant to build.

## Keep it current when you publish

The failure mode is a feed that was true at launch and then froze. The file still validates. The last item is eight months old. Anyone who subscribed during a busy month now has a reader that implies you stopped. Sometimes you did stop, and the feed is right to say so. More often the essays kept shipping and nobody wired the feed to the publish action. That is a broken promise, not a quiet season.

Tie the feed to the same event as the public page. When a draft becomes an article, the item appears. When you unpublish, the item disappears. When you change the slug, redirect the article and do not leave the feed pointing at the old path. A reader full of 404s is a louder resignation than an empty file.

On a Next.js site this is an ordinary route that reads the same posts the blog index reads, and prints them as XML. It does not need a third CMS. It should not include portal pages, client files, or anything behind a login. Hanabi keeps the public marketing site separate from the authenticated portal. The feed is public. If a piece is not public, it is not in the feed. That rule is simple enough to keep under pressure, which is the only kind of rule that survives a launch week.

Preview deployments should not advertise a second feed. A subscriber who accidentally followed a preview host will get drafts, broken links, and a view of work you did not mean to show. Production is the feed. Everything else can be noindex, or absent.

## The small promise

What you are promising is modest, which is why it works. You are not promising a weekly masterpiece. You are promising that published work will be listed, in order, at a stable address. A founder who cares about your point of view can keep that address and ignore you the rest of the time. When you do publish, you do not have to hope they were online that afternoon.

The promise has a tone. Two or three finished pieces in a week, if that is truly your pace, will show up as two or three items. A hundred thin posts in a day will show up as a flood, and the reader will mark the feed as noise. The feed does not create the cadence. It reveals it. If you are embarrassed by what the file would look like, you are embarrassed by the publishing plan, and you should change the plan rather than hide the file.

Write items the way you write pages. Short sentences. A concrete claim. No "in case you missed it" stacked on top of a post that is still on the homepage. No false urgency. A studio that sounds careful on the site and breathless in the feed has two brands. Subscribers notice, because the feed is often the only surface they see.

There is also a promise to yourself. A feed is a log. Six months later you can see whether you published what you said the studio knew. The gaps are informative. A gap where a service has no essays is a gap in the work or in the writing. A cluster of near-duplicates is visible as a run of titles that could be swapped. Use that view in an editorial meeting. It is harsher than a content calendar and more honest.

## What to leave out

Leave out full text if the full text includes anything you would not want copied into a third-party reader cache forever. A summary plus a link is enough for most studio essays. Leave out tracking parameters on the link. Leave out items that are only there to pad the file, such as tag pages, author archives, and "hello world." Leave out categories you do not actually write. An empty category feed that 404s or returns a stub looks like a product you abandoned.

Leave out the client portal, proposals, and anything with a customer's name that was not cleared for a public case study. The public projects Hanabi names, Down the Cove, Thomas Bewick, Ballarat Box Sports, Wabisabi, Got Next, Leadly, Trade Moai, are public. A feed is not the place to widen that list because a file felt sparse.

If you run a podcast or a changelog later, give it its own feed or be very clear in the title what kind of item it is. Mixing "new essay" and "we changed a dependency" in one undifferentiated stream trains people to skip both. A studio blog can stay a studio blog.

Also leave out a second, secret feed for "the good posts." If a post is not good enough for subscribers, it is not good enough to publish. The discipline is the point.

## How a reader actually uses it

Assume a skeptical person. They find the feed because you linked it in the footer with the words "RSS" or "Follow," not because you hid a pink icon and hoped. They add it. For a month, nothing they see should surprise them relative to the site. Same titles. Same order. Working links.

When they click, they should land on the article, not on the homepage, and not on a page that begs them to subscribe again. They already subscribed. The page can offer the next related essay in a sentence, the way any good page does. It does not need a second capture form above the answer.

If you change the feed URL, redirect the old one. Feed addresses are bookmarks. Breaking them is like changing the studio's phone number and disconnecting the old line. Put the new address in the old file if you must move, and keep the redirect for a long time. Longer than feels necessary.

Check the file the way you check a page. It should parse. It should list the latest posts. The dates should be plausible. The links should be the canonical ones. Open one item in a reader, or in a browser if you do not use a reader, and confirm the summary is the summary you would say out loud.

## A footer link is enough

You do not need a campaign around the feed. A visible link in the footer, and maybe at the bottom of the blog index, is the whole advertisement. Label it with what the person gets: new writing, in a reader, without an account. If almost nobody uses it, that is still fine. The cost of keeping it true is low, and the people who use it are often the ones who read closely enough to become a conversation.

The site around the feed still has to be worth following. [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) are the design and build of that site: the public pages, the writing, and the engineering that keeps a small promise like a feed from going stale after launch.

A feed names the pieces. It does not, by itself, say who stands behind them. [Author pages that are real](/blog/author-pages-that-are-real) is the next piece, because a subscriber who trusts the writing will eventually ask whose practice it is, and "Admin" is not an answer.
